title: Polynomial neural surrogates for designing photonic quantum experiments
abstract: Physics simulators can support the discovery of quantum experiments by predicting the states generated by experimental configurations. When these simulators are computationally expensive, repeated simulator calls can limit the search for experiments that generate a desired quantum state. Here, we develop a physics-inspired polynomial neural surrogate for PyTheus, a graph-based quantum-optics simulator, to predict quantum states and use it to design quantum experiments. Its polynomial activations are motivated by the relation between graph perfect matchings and the resulting state amplitudes. We train separate surrogate models for four-, six-, and eight-photon systems and show that they achieve higher prediction accuracy with fewer trainable parameters than standard multilayer perceptrons. We then use the trained surrogates for inverse design of GHZ, W, and linear-cluster states. For the larger systems, the surrogates also enable faster inverse design than direct optimization with PyTheus. These results suggest that incorporating the underlying physics into neural surrogates can provide an efficient approach to quantum experiment design.
summary: This paper introduces a Polynomial Neural Surrogate (PNN) to accelerate the prediction of quantum states in photonic quantum experiments. By embedding the known polynomial structure of the underlying physics into the neural network, the PNN outperforms standard MLPs in accuracy and efficiency. This breakthrough allows for significantly faster inverse design of complex quantum states for larger systems.
main_problem: The core problem is developing efficient methods to predict quantum states generated by photonic quantum experiments when the underlying simulator is computationally expensive.
main_result: A physics-inspired Polynomial Neural Surrogate (PNN) was developed that achieves higher prediction accuracy with fewer parameters than standard MLPs, enabling faster inverse design of target quantum states for larger systems.
method: The authors train a PNN to approximate the graph-to-state amplitude mapping, and then use this surrogate model to iteratively optimize graph weights for inverse design.
model_or_system: The system involves photonic quantum experiments modeled by PyTheus, which uses weighted graphs where quantum state amplitudes are calculated via sums over perfect matchings of the graph structure.
key_observables: Unnormalized output-state amplitudes, state fidelity ($F(x)$), and Jacobian sensitivities ($\mathbf{J}$).
important_parameters: System size ($n=4, 6, 8$ photons), graph weights ($\mathbf{w}$), and optimization loss parameters ($\lambda_1$).
main_assumptions: The PNN structure is motivated by the known polynomial nature of the graph-to-state amplitude mapping, although it does not explicitly encode individual perfect matchings.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the graph representation and perfect matching contributions; subsequent figures show training/validation MAE curves, fidelity distributions comparing initial vs. final states, and Jacobian sensitivity comparisons between the PNN and analytical results.
paper_structure: The paper introduces the problem, details the PNN architecture and training against an MLP baseline, demonstrates the PNN's superior accuracy and parameter efficiency, and finally applies the trained surrogate for fast inverse design of specific target states (GHZ, W, LC).
why_interesting: This work directly addresses the computational bottleneck in quantum optics simulations, providing a scalable, physics-informed machine learning tool for quantum state engineering.

figures.caption: FIG. 1. Graph representation and perfect matching contributions. (a) Fully connected four-vertex graph. Blue and red colours represent the photon states |0⟩and |1⟩, respec- tively. An edge joining vertices a and b with photon states i and j has weight wij ab ∈[−1, 1]. The four colour combinations for each of the six vertex pairs give 24 weights, collected in the vector x. Diamonds indicate negative weights. (b) For n = 4, three perfect matchings contribute to the |1111⟩am- plitude. A perfect matching is a set of edges that covers every vertex exactly once. Summing the contributions from these three matchings gives the amplitude in the unnormalised out- put state: ⟨1111|Ψpost⟩= w11 01w11 23...

FIG. 2. Surrogate training and inverse design. (a) Sur- rogate training. A weighted graph, encoded by the graph- weight vector x, is passed through the neural network to predict the corresponding quantum-state amplitudes |ΨNN⟩. (b) Surrogate-assisted inverse design. A randomly initialised graph-weight vector x is passed through the trained model, with its weights and biases frozen. The graph weights are it- eratively updated to maximize the target evaluated from the predicted state until the stopping criterion is reached.

FIG. 3. Training and validation loss curves for the PNN and FNN surrogate models for n = 4, 6, and 8. The mean absolute error (MAE) between the predicted and PyTheus-generated unnormalised output states is shown on a logarithmic scale. Across all system sizes, the PNN achieves a lower validation loss than the MLP. For n = 8, MLP training stopped after 2000 epochs without further improvement. The best validation losses for all architectures and system sizes are reported in Table I.

FIG. 4. Test-set prediction errors of the trained PNN surrogates. Distributions of the sample-wise mean absolute error (MAE) for the (a) n = 4, (b) n = 6, and (c) n = 8 systems. Each histogram contains all two million samples from the corresponding held-out test set. For each sample, the MAE is the mean absolute difference between the PNN-predicted and PyTheus-generated unnormalised output-state amplitudes over all output components. The red vertical line indicates the mean sample-wise MAE for each system size. The horizontal axes are shown in units of 10−6.

FIG. 5. Jacobian sensitivity comparison for n = 4. (a) Mean absolute sensitivities from the PNN (left) and analytical perfect-matching calculation (right), averaged over 1000 sampled graphs. (b) Absolute element-wise difference between the two sensitivity matrices. The similar patterns and small differences show that the PNN reproduces the sensitivity of the output amplitudes to variations in the graph weights
